title: hp-Adaptive Finite Element Modeling of Static Cracks in Density-Dependent Media
authors: Vicente Valle Martinez, Saugata Ghosh, S. M. Mallikarjunaiah, Dambaru Bhatta
abstract: The elastostatic crack-tip fields within a density-dependent continuum are numerically investigated under several macroscopic loading configurations. The governing nonlinear boundary value problem is formulated using an algebraically nonlinear hyperelastic constitutive relationship in which the material moduli are intrinsically coupled to volumetric strain. Existence and uniqueness of the weak solution to the nonlinear displacement-based variational formulation are rigorously established at the continuous level via the Minty-Browder theorem. The variational formulation is then linearized at the partial differential equation level to construct a continuous damped Newton-Raphson scheme. To accurately capture the severe field gradients and internal singularities inherent to this model, the resulting sequence of linear operator equations is discretized and solved via a conforming finite element method within an $hp$-adaptive framework. A comparative analysis is conducted across five distinct boundary loading profiles (encompassing uniform, piecewise-slope, and concentrated point loads) applied to a stationary cracked geometry. Within each configuration, the density-dependent constitutive parameter is systematically varied to assess its regulatory impact on the fracture process zone, focusing on the spatial evolution of normal stress, normal strain, and strain energy density near the crack tip. Numerical results demonstrate that local kinematic deformability is strictly bounded by the strain-limiting nature of the continuum, whereby static equilibrium is sustained through severe, localized stress amplifications. Furthermore, the mechanical influence of the modeling parameter is fundamentally dictated by the topological interplay between internal crack geometry and the spatial distribution of applied macroscopic loads.

infographic.key_insight: The density-dependent, strain-limiting continuum bounds local deformation near static crack tips while sustaining equilibrium through highly localized stress amplification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model helps engineers examine how load placement and density-dependent constitutive behavior reshape near-tip stress, strain, and energy concentrations.
method: Formulate nonlinear hyperelastic equilibrium with material moduli coupled to volumetric strain.
Establish weak-solution existence and uniqueness using the Minty–Browder theorem.
Solve with a damped Newton–Raphson scheme and conforming hp-adaptive finite elements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical comparisons span five loading profiles and variations of the density-dependent parameter, tracking near-tip normal stress, normal strain, and strain energy density.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract evaluates stationary cracks numerically; it does not report experimental validation or demonstrate crack-growth prediction.
infographic.paper_title: hp-Adaptive Finite Element Modeling of Static Cracks in Density-Dependent Media

title: Large-deformation constitutive modeling of viscoelastic foams: Application to an open-cell foam material
authors: Jialiang Tao, Alexander K. Landauer, Zicheng Yan, Xiuqi Li, Christian Franck, David L Henann
abstract: Open-cell elastomeric foams are widely utilized for impact protection and cushioning applications. These foams can demonstrate remarkable elastic compressibility and rate sensitivity over a wide range of force and acceleration protection levels. They often exhibit volumetric-distortional coupling in their mechanical response and potentially compaction banding when subjected to dynamic loads. Here, a phenomenological modeling framework, adopted previously for closed-cell foams, is specified using an experimental characterization-based approach for calibrating and validating the large-deformation, viscoelastic material model. Homogeneous simple compression and tension experiments were performed on isotropic, open-cell viscoelastic foam materials, and stress-strain and lateral-axial strain data were used for model calibration. Data were collected at decadal strain rates to inform the rate-sensitive aspects of the model. The modeling approach involved decomposing the total material response into an equilibrium hyperelastic contribution and several nonlinear, Maxwell-like contributions and utilized invariants of the logarithmic strain to account for large deformations and the strong volumetric-distortional coupling effect. A new strain localization detection algorithm was developed and used to check for the formation of compaction bands, which would invalidate modeling assumptions for the calibration experiments. To validate the predictive capability of the constitutive model, experiments were conducted that involved intentionally inhomogeneous deformations over a spectrum of strain rates and deformation types. The consistency between the measured responses from the validation experiments and the model predictions obtained from finite-element-based numerical simulations was largely within the experimental uncertainty bounds, demonstrating the predictive capability of the model.

infographic.key_insight: A large-deformation viscoelastic model captures open-cell foam’s rate-sensitive response and volumetric–distortional coupling, with validation predictions largely within experimental uncertainty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports finite-element prediction of foam deformation for cushioning and impact-protection design.
method: Combine equilibrium hyperelasticity with multiple nonlinear Maxwell-like contributions.
Use logarithmic-strain invariants to represent large deformations and volumetric–distortional coupling.
Calibrate with compression, tension, and lateral-strain data across decadal strain rates; screen for compaction bands.
infographic.evidence_signal: Finite-element predictions were tested against intentionally inhomogeneous experiments spanning strain rates and deformation types, with agreement largely within experimental uncertainty bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Compaction-band formation can invalidate the homogeneous-deformation assumptions used for calibration and requires explicit screening.
infographic.paper_title: Large-deformation constitutive modeling of viscoelastic foams: Application to an open-cell foam material

title: Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet with IFENN: A Generalized Framework for Coupled Poroelasticity Problems
authors: Fouad M. Amin, Rigoberto Moncada, Panos Pantidis, Diab W. Abueidda, Fan Fei, Mostafa E. Mobasher
abstract: Complex, high-dimensional, large-scale poroelasticity simulations using traditional numerical solvers can be prohibitively expensive in terms of computational resources. We introduce an innovative framework for poroelasticity problems that integrates physics-informed machine learning (PI-ML) models with high-performance FEM solvers. This integration is achieved through the Integrated Finite Element Neural Network (IFENN) setup, which uses a staggered scheme between an FEM solver for mechanical equilibrium and a PI-ML model for fluid-flow predictions. We introduce a novel Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet (PIF-MIONet) architecture, in which a fusion network encodes the outputs of the MIONet branches. The MIONet encodes different input functions, and the fusion network enables early interaction between the inputs, supporting generalization across multiple scenarios while adhering to the underlying physics of the poroelasticity problem. We study different examples, covering 2D and 3D domains and considering variable material properties and time discretizations. We test the models on unseen loading histories, demonstrating accuracy and generalizability across scenarios. For complex geometries and boundary conditions, we show that with both physics and data considered in the loss function, a PI-ML model can be trained using only 0.1\% of the training increments used for pure data-driven training. In addition, we expand the PIF-MIONet to incorporate a domain decomposition approach, which was found to be particularly useful when modeling flow over more complex geometries with more localized phenomena. For the first time, IFENN is implemented using the open-source multiphysics simulator GEOS for the FEM part, providing a path for the framework's application to industrial-scale simulations and complex multiphysics problems.

infographic.key_insight: PIF-MIONet combines multi-input neural operators with physics-informed learning inside IFENN to predict fluid flow while FEM solves mechanical equilibrium in coupled poroelasticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Integration with the open-source GEOS simulator offers a path toward efficient poroelastic simulations for complex geometries and industrial-scale multiphysics.
method: Stagger FEM mechanical-equilibrium solves with neural fluid-flow predictions.
Fuse MIONet branch outputs to enable early interaction among input functions.
Combine physics and data losses, with domain decomposition for localized flow phenomena.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests span 2D and 3D domains, variable material properties, time discretizations, and unseen loading histories; for complex cases, physics-and-data training used only 0.1% of the training increments used by pure data-driven training.
infographic.watch_item: Industrial-scale speedups and robustness beyond the tested scenarios are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet with IFENN: A Generalized Framework for Coupled Poroelasticity Problems

title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness
authors: Ke Tan, Chong-Jun Li, Xu Guo
abstract: Problem-independent machine learning (PIML) is an effective computational approach that combines the finite element method with machine learning. PIML uses neural networks to learn the mapping from material distributions or element geometries to the numerical shape functions of substructures. This approach avoids repeated computation while preserving the conformity of the underlying finite element discretization, thereby significantly improving the efficiency of substructure-based finite element analysis. However, existing studies on PIML have primarily focused on numerical accuracy and computational efficiency, while rigorous theoretical analyses of its approximation errors are still limited. In this paper, we establish an error analysis framework for PIML from a classical finite element perspective, in which the numerical error is bounded in terms of the finite element discretization error and the network generalization error. Our analysis shows that, when only rigid-body displacement invariance is enforced, the resulting error estimate contains a learning-induced term that does not necessarily decrease under mesh refinement. To ensure convergence, we propose an improved PIML scheme with linear completeness. By using linear displacement field constraints to reconstruct the corresponding columns of the transition matrix, we ensure that the resulting numerical shape-function space contains the space of linear polynomials. We derive error estimates and establish convergence results of the improved scheme in the H1 and L2 norms. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate that the improved PIML achieves optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.

infographic.key_insight: Enforcing linear completeness in PIML removes a key obstacle to mesh-refinement convergence and supports rigorous H1 and L2 error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can accelerate substructure-based finite element analysis while preserving conformity and improving convergence reliability.
method: Train neural networks to map material distributions or element geometries to substructure numerical shape functions.
Reconstruct transition-matrix columns using linear displacement constraints to ensure linear completeness.
Bound numerical error through finite element discretization and network generalization errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.
infographic.watch_item: Linear completeness addresses convergence consistency, but practical accuracy still depends on network generalization to the target materials and geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness

title: Projector Subspace Optimization for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
authors: Hao Yu, Quan Cheng, Lijun Zhang
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet adapting them to sequential tasks requires Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). Existing replay-free methods expand prompts or routed LoRA experts across multi-layer decoders, incurring heavy parameter and routing overhead while shifting internal feature distributions. Instead, we identify the final linear layer of the vision-language projector as a high-capacity, coordinate-stationary bridge, where sequential updates easily induce interface drift by displacing historical visual tokens. While low-rank subspace adaptation offers a compact remedy, selecting directions solely from historical statistics or task gradients sacrifices plasticity or stability, and unconstrained multi-step updates still accumulate large drift. To resolve both issues, we propose Projector Refinement through Optimized Update Directions (PROUD), a continual subspace optimization framework for the terminal projector layer. At task onset, PROUD combines retained input statistics with initial gradients to analytically extract a metric-orthonormal subspace maximizing first-order task gain under a drift budget. During training, it regularizes updates within this fixed subspace via an exact Frobenius penalty before losslessly merging them with zero inference or routing overhead. Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones show that PROUD outperforms recent replay-free baselines in continual accuracy while curbing forgetting with a fraction of trainable parameters.

infographic.key_insight: PROUD reduces forgetting in multimodal continual instruction tuning by optimizing a compact update subspace in the vision–language projector’s final linear layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support sequential adaptation of engineering vision–language assistants with low training overhead, but solid-mechanics applications are not evaluated in the abstract.
method: Combine retained input statistics and initial task gradients to select a metric-orthonormal subspace balancing task gain against interface drift.
Train within the fixed subspace using an exact Frobenius penalty to constrain drift.
Losslessly merge updates into the projector with no added inference or routing overhead.
infographic.evidence_signal: On UCIT and CoIN across multiple MLLM backbones, the abstract reports higher continual accuracy and less forgetting than recent replay-free baselines, using a fraction of their trainable parameters.
infographic.watch_item: A subspace fixed at task onset may become less aligned with useful update directions as training progresses; the abstract provides no quantitative sensitivity analysis.
infographic.paper_title: Projector Subspace Optimization for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning

title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
authors: Hongrui Chen, Kittipong Thiamchaiboonthawee, Zhen Wei, Amin Heyrani Nobari, Faez Ahmed
abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.

infographic.key_insight: OAT3D generates high-resolution 3D structural topologies using a generative model designed to accommodate varying domain shapes, resolutions, loads, and supports.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It accelerates structural topology optimization, reporting a 3.65× speedup over conventional optimization when targeting similar compliance.
method: Sparsely encode load and fixity conditions.
Represent structures with a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder.
Generate candidate topologies using a conditional diffusion transformer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training data comprise 501,865 optimized topologies generated using 51,800 GPU-hours; OAT3D generates structures at 512³ resolution with a reported 44.9× speedup for raw candidate generation.
infographic.watch_item: Raw generation speed does not imply equivalent structural performance; generated candidates still warrant finite element verification.
infographic.paper_title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization

title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
authors: Xiang Meng, Shuhei Shinzato, Zhiqiang Zhao, Linfeng Yu, Jian Guo, Liangli Chu
abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $γ/α_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $α_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.

infographic.key_insight: Boron redistributes toward defects in TiAl, locally pinning dislocations and suppressing deformation twinning to strengthen the alloy at high temperature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling boron content and defect structure could improve high-temperature TiAl strength, while brittle borides and interface-dependent adhesion require careful management.
method: Develop a high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential.
Simulate boron redistribution using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics.
Analyze defect interactions, tensile deformation, and stacking-fault energetics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Polycrystalline TiAl simulations show a 9.4% increase in average flow stress at 1 at.% B and 900 K, accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation.
infographic.watch_item: The strengthening result is simulation-based; experimental validation and transferability across alloy compositions and processing conditions remain important.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys

title: Constrained Allen-Cahn phase-field topology optimization of flexoelectric devices
authors: Hao Zhen, Sheng Mao
abstract: Topology optimization provides an effective approach to exploring performance-oriented designs for miniature devices. In this work, a phase-field framework for constrained topology optimization of microscale flexoelectric devices is developed using a continuum model under the assumption of infinitesimal deformations. The material distribution is optimized at the device level with the output voltage as the objective. The framework also accommodates objectives based on capacitance or stored electrostatic energy. Manufacturing variations are incorporated through a worst-case objective over the prescribed geometric realizations, with spectral constraints imposed to maintain the structural connectivity. The framework is applied to two-dimensional pressure and bending sensors and a three-dimensional thin-film device. The optimized nominal output voltages reach approximately 4.8 times the initial value for the pressure sensor and 2.5-3.4 times the initial values for the bending sensors. The voltage gains arise primarily from increased mechanically induced source charge, with capacitance reduction providing an additional contribution that varies with the device configuration. Erosion analyses of representative designs further show that structural connectivity is well preserved when structural members become locally narrower, with the output voltage remaining close to that of the nominal configuration. Combined with specific microfabrication processes, this optimization framework is expected to provide a numerical basis for configuration screening and prototype development of flexoelectric devices.

infographic.key_insight: Constrained phase-field topology optimization boosts flexoelectric sensor voltage primarily by increasing mechanically induced source charge, with additional gains from reduced capacitance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports performance-driven design of microscale flexoelectric devices while accounting for manufacturing variations and structural connectivity.
method: Optimize material distribution using a constrained Allen–Cahn phase-field framework and an infinitesimal-deformation continuum model.
Maximize output voltage, with support for capacitance or stored electrostatic energy objectives.
Address manufacturing variations through worst-case geometric realizations and spectral connectivity constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies cover 2D pressure and bending sensors and a 3D thin-film device; nominal voltage reaches approximately 4.8× the initial value for the pressure sensor and 2.5–3.4× for bending sensors.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical results rather than experimental validation; fabrication-specific feasibility and performance remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Constrained Allen-Cahn phase-field topology optimization of flexoelectric devices

title: A mixed-primal FEM for Poisson-Fermi interfacial problems
authors: Siyad Rahman Mandottil, Neela Nataraj, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier
abstract: This paper presents a mixed-primal FEM for a linearised Poisson--Fermi interface problem arising from the Bazant--Storey--Kornyshev theory, which describes electrostatic interactions in ionic solutions. It leads to a transmission problem coupling a fourth-order equation in the solvent region with a second-order equation in the solute region. To precisely compute the electrostatic stress and the interactive force in the electrolyte, we reformulate the fourth-order problem as a mixed system by introducing the gradient of the electrostatic potential, the divergence of its gradient, and the gradient of its divergence as additional independent variables. The second-order problem is studied in its primal form as this approach eliminates the requirement for Lagrange multipliers to enforce the transmission conditions. The resulting formulation is discretised using Raviart--Thomas finite elements for the vector variables and piecewise polynomial finite elements for the scalar variables. Well-posedness of the mixed-primal formulation and optimal a priori error estimates for the field variables as well as for the postprocessed Maxwell tensor are established under suitable regularity assumptions, in parameter-weighted norms in which the inf-sup constant is independent of the correlation length and of the permittivity ratio. The constants in the error estimates are independent of both parameters as well, up to a loss of at most half an order when the mesh does not resolve the length scale (square root of the relative permittivity); the Sobolev norms of the solution may still depend on the parameters through boundary layers. The postprocessed Maxwell stress converges with optimal order on quasi-uniform meshes, except for the lowest-order scheme in 3D. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the properties of the proposed method for problems in 2D and 3D.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed-primal FEM couples fourth-order solvent electrostatics with a second-order solute model, enabling accurate field and Maxwell stress approximation with parameter-robust error bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate electrostatic stress and interaction-force calculations support simulations of ionic solutions and electrolyte–solute interfaces.
method: Introduce potential-gradient, divergence, and divergence-gradient variables in the solvent.
Retain a primal solute formulation to enforce transmission conditions without Lagrange multipliers.
Discretise vector fields with Raviart–Thomas elements and scalar fields with piecewise polynomials.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments in 2D and 3D validate theoretical convergence rates, including optimal postprocessed Maxwell stress convergence on quasi-uniform meshes except for the lowest-order 3D scheme.
infographic.watch_item: Unresolved parameter-dependent length scales can reduce convergence by up to half an order, and boundary layers may still make solution regularity parameter-dependent.
infographic.paper_title: A mixed-primal FEM for Poisson-Fermi interfacial problems

title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
authors: Ziyue Peng, Yanxi Hu, Junyoung Kim, Andrew Chen, Jin Yang, Chandrajit L. Bajaj
abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.

infographic.key_insight: Short 2D motion tracklets transfer better than depth-lifted 3D tracklets for estimating deformable-object materials from real drop videos, reversing their ranking in simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single drop video can support rapid estimation of density-normalized stiffness and, when plastic deformation occurs, density-normalized yield stress.
method: Train the feed-forward PhysReader predictor entirely in simulation.
Combine video with short 2D optical-flow tracklets.
Learn a 3D representation by matching a teacher with access to exact 3D deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PhysReader-Real—16 everyday objects with five drops each and jointly fitted reference materials checked against tensile tests—PhysReader outperformed all compared inputs and baselines except an optimizer initialized from its predictions, which took 49 minutes per video versus 12 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Synthetic validation can misrank real-world performance; even accurate depth did not resolve the transfer failure of depth-lifted 3D tracklets.
infographic.paper_title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video

title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models
authors: Yicheng Huang, Feng Ke, Linhan Chen, Ziyi Jiang, Xiu Yin Zhang
abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 < 0$). We present PhysRF-WorldJEPA, a manifold-decoupled Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that separates continuous electromagnetic state prediction from cross-modal language alignment. An unattenuated 1.0x clock anchor and parallel dual-scale RF encoder feed a lean ~3% LoRA LLM trained with two-step state-space EMA-JEPA (Denoise -> Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.

infographic.key_insight: Separating radar-state prediction from language alignment improves radar-to-text retrieval without degrading continuous physical-state estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports privacy-preserving motion and scene monitoring during sensor blackouts and through visual obstructions, though fracture or material-damage assessment is not demonstrated.
method: Encode radar streams with a dual-scale RF encoder and clock anchor feeding an LLM with approximately 3% LoRA adaptation.
Learn continuous states using two-step EMA-JEPA denoising and rollout, plus Batch-VICReg, to predict 3 seconds ahead.
Freeze the physical backbone and train a stop-gradient language-alignment head with false-negative masking.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 4,541 radar windows across three domains against 10 baselines, the decoupled head increased radar-to-text R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% while preserving physical readouts, including 3.37° torso-tilt error at a 3-second blackout horizon.
infographic.watch_item: Blackout-prediction gains vary by LLM family and representation, so transfer to new sensors and engineering monitoring tasks needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models

title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning
authors: Shanmuga Venkatachalam, Quinn Jacobson, John Paul Shen
abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

infographic.key_insight: NeuTNN-AV achieves competitive audio-visual classification using 4-bit spiking networks with far fewer synapses than leading SNN baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its comparison-and-addition inference supports resource-constrained multimodal sensing, though the abstract does not evaluate solid mechanics applications.
method: Encode inputs temporally, with each input line spiking at most once.
Use neurons with multiple active dendritic segments and local reward-modulated STDP learning.
Store weights as 4-bit integers and perform inference using only comparisons and additions.
infographic.evidence_signal: NeuTNN-AV reports 78.6% accuracy on CREMA-D with 2.34M synapses and 98.82% on UrbanSound8K-AV with 1.38M, plus 23–106× smaller weight memory than spiking baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Reported synaptic energy savings do not establish end-to-end system efficiency; preprocessing and hardware overhead require validation.
infographic.paper_title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
authors: Konstantinos Dovelos
abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

infographic.key_insight: An independent certificate checker gives guaranteed error bounds for PDE solver outputs, including finite-element solutions and neural predictions, without trusting the solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-based certificates can help validate automated simulation pipelines and learned surrogates when convergence alone misses incorrect solutions.
method: Return an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current alongside each prediction.
Use a small independent checker to bound error against the stated physics model.
Evaluate conventional solvers, deliberately buggy and LLM-written code, and neural surrogates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The checker rejected or refuted all five convergent buggy solvers and gave reduced-basis neural predictions certified intervals at most 0.0021% wide in-range and 0.3–25% wide out-of-range.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees apply to the stated model, but bounds can be uninformative unless outputs are energy-accurate on a grid that resolves the problem.
infographic.paper_title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates

title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction
authors: Yuan Zhang, Mohammad Amin Nabian, Shaotong Fu, Yiding Liu, Chengcheng Chu, Xuelin Tao
abstract: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.

infographic.key_insight: Topology-guided regional latent dynamics enable accurate full-field prediction of transient nonlinear structural responses on large finite element meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate targets time-history prediction for heterogeneous structures, including stiffened panels and million-node vehicle crash models.
method: Encode mesh responses into regional latent states using engineering priors and topology-constrained interactions.
Improve latent dynamics with auxiliary one-step prediction and forecast trajectories using load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba.
Reconstruct full-field nodal responses with a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on three FEM datasets, TPLD reports 1.41%–12.22% displacement-component relative L2 errors on an approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle and 0.620% position error on the BIW benchmark, 30.7% below the best GeoTransolver configuration.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to unseen structural topologies and loading regimes is not established by the abstract; regional partitioning also requires mesh and engineering priors.
infographic.paper_title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction

title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows
authors: Harald Garcke, Yifei Li, Robert Nürnberg, Quan Zhao
abstract: We introduce a geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation for the $L^2$-gradient flow of a class of curvature-dependent energies of closed hypersurfaces, where the energy density depends on the mean curvature and the unit normal. A square-root auxiliary variable converts the geometric energy into a quadratic functional. Combining its evolution equation with a skew-symmetric treatment of surface transport yields a weak formulation whose energy law depends only on the normal velocity and is therefore independent of the chosen tangential motion. We construct monolithic nonlinear parametric finite element methods by coupling a common IEQ discretization with one of two geometric formulations that accommodate either the Barrett-Garcke-Nürnberg (BGN) tangential velocity or the minimal-deformation-rate (MDR) tangential velocity. Both fully discrete approximations satisfy an unconditional decay estimate for the discrete quadratic energy. We further extend the construction to anisotropic Willmore flow, and to $H^{-1}$-gradient flows. A variety of numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of the introduced methods.

infographic.key_insight: A geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation enables curvature-driven surface evolution with unconditional discrete energy decay, independent of tangential motion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports energy-stable finite element simulation of evolving interfaces governed by curvature-dependent energies.
method: Introduce a square-root auxiliary variable to express the geometric energy as a quadratic functional.
Use skew-symmetric surface transport so the energy law depends only on normal velocity.
Construct monolithic nonlinear parametric FEM schemes with BGN or minimal-deformation-rate tangential motion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports unconditional discrete energy decay for both schemes and numerical experiments demonstrating robustness and accuracy, without quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Unconditional energy decay does not guarantee time-step-independent accuracy; the monolithic nonlinear schemes also require nonlinear solves.
infographic.paper_title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows

title: Sparse Constitutive Neural Networks for Hyperelasticity
authors: Hendrik Geisler, Clément Jailin, Emmanuel Baranger
abstract: Constitutive model identification aims to recover compact, interpretable models that accurately describe material behavior. In this work, we identify hyperelastic constitutive models using artificial neural networks with sparsity-promoting constraints and regularization. The proposed method combines the expressiveness of neural networks with the structural interpretability of sparse constitutive models, such as those identified by EUCLID, by representing the strain energy density as a sum of products of univariate functions of the invariants. The resulting decomposition exposes the contributions of individual invariants and their interactions. The method is demonstrated on synthetic data in supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios, showing that it can accurately identify interpretable constitutive models with few active modes.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse neural networks identify compact hyperelastic strain-energy models while exposing individual invariant contributions and their interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support interpretable material-law identification for solid-mechanics simulations.
method: Represent strain-energy density as a sum of products of univariate functions of invariants.
Apply sparsity-promoting constraints and regularization to retain few active modes.
Identify constitutive models in supervised and unsupervised learning settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic-data demonstrations report accurate, interpretable constitutive models with few active modes in both learning settings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports only synthetic-data validation, leaving robustness to noisy experimental measurements unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Constitutive Neural Networks for Hyperelasticity

title: Bayesian Calibration of Effective Material Parameters in Electric Machine Stators
authors: Patrick D. Gsoels, Christian M. Riener, Markus Flicker, Jose Romero Lopera, Jan P. Henninger, Bibhu Prasad Nayak
abstract: Efficiency-driven faster switching by wide-bandgap semiconductor devices increases electromagnetic interference (EMI) in electric vehicles (EVs). Mitigating this EMI becomes more complex as system components grow. Therefore, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is assessed early via system-level simulation of the EV powertrain. A key EMC-critical quantity is the impedance of the electric drive machine, forming a major part of the EMI propagation path. Finite element (FE) simulations are typically used but are computationally expensive and limited by insufficient material property knowledge. We present a surrogate model based Bayesian calibration framework for 3D full-wave FE simulation of an externally excited synchronous motor (EESM) stator. Effective material parameters (EMPs) are calibrated to match broadband differential mode (DM) impedance measurements up to 30 MHz. A multi-output surrogate model replaces the demanding FE simulation, while an orthogonal surrogate model compliant discrepancy term assesses material modeling completeness. Using Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo, we construct posterior distributions of the EMPs for three calibration scenarios with different parameter ranges. Two of three scenarios achieve good agreement with measurements. However, accurate calibration requires "datasheet-deviating" EMPs, while "datasheet-aligned" ones yield deficient results, indicating material models do not fully capture the underlying physics. The proposed methodology enables estimating unknown material properties from impedance measurements and evaluates the sufficiency of chosen material models. Although identified EMPs may differ from datasheet values, they reliably estimate frequency-dependent DM impedance. This work focuses on EMPs influencing the stator's DM impedance; complete machine calibration, including rotor and common-mode impedance, is the scope of future research.

infographic.key_insight: Surrogate-assisted Bayesian calibration matches stator differential-mode impedance, but successful fits require effective material parameters that deviate from datasheet values.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports early EV powertrain EMC assessment by estimating broadband machine impedance while reducing reliance on costly full-wave FE simulations.
method: Replace 3D full-wave stator FE simulations with a multi-output surrogate.
Calibrate effective material parameters using Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo.
Use an orthogonal surrogate-compliant discrepancy term to assess material-model completeness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against measured differential-mode impedance up to 30 MHz, two of three parameter-range scenarios achieved good agreement; datasheet-aligned parameters produced deficient results.
infographic.watch_item: Calibrated parameters are effective rather than necessarily physical material properties; rotor and common-mode impedance calibration remain future work.
infographic.paper_title: Bayesian Calibration of Effective Material Parameters in Electric Machine Stators

title: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning
authors: Shivanand Kundargi, Kowshik Thopalli, Tejas Gokhale
abstract: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.

infographic.key_insight: SACK prioritizes incoming samples by their semantic relationship to previously learned concepts, improving continual learning while reducing forgetting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SACK could support engineering models that learn sequentially from new datasets, although the abstract does not demonstrate solid mechanics or constitutive modeling applications.
method: Decompose learned categorical knowledge into fine-grained concepts.
Compute relationships between previously learned and incoming concepts.
Use concept relationships to prioritize new samples within existing continual learning methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments with regularization-, replay-, and prompt-based methods in class- and task-incremental settings report improved accuracy, reduced forgetting, and better calibration and robustness, without numerical results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify the computational overhead of concept extraction and sample prioritization.
infographic.paper_title: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning

title: A decoupled BDF2-type integrator for the spin-diffusion Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert system in ferromagnetic multilayers
authors: Michele Aldé, Dirk Praetorius, Agus L. Soenjaya
abstract: We propose and analyze a fully discrete, linear, decoupled BDF2-type finite element integrator for the spin-diffusion Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert (SDLLG) system arising in spintronics. The SDLLG equations couple the magnetization dynamics with a diffusion equation for spin accumulation. The proposed numerical method combines a projection-free BDF2-type tangent-plane discretization of the magnetization dynamics with BDF2 time-stepping for the spin accumulation. By treating the coupling terms explicitly through extrapolation, each time step requires only two independent linear solves that can be performed in parallel. The analysis accommodates the usual exchange field and a general, possibly nonlinear, lower-order effective field. Unconditional weak convergence towards a global weak solution is shown. We also establish bounds on the deviation from the unit-length constraint. Under additional assumptions on the associated energy functional, an energy inequality for the limiting solution is obtained. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: A linear, decoupled BDF2-type finite element integrator advances coupled magnetization and spin diffusion using two independent linear solves per time step.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports parallel simulation of spin dynamics in ferromagnetic multilayers relevant to spintronic device modeling.
method: Projection-free BDF2-type tangent-plane discretization for magnetization.
BDF2 time-stepping for spin accumulation.
Explicit extrapolation of coupling terms enables parallel linear solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper proves unconditional weak convergence and bounds on unit-length constraint deviation, with numerical experiments supporting the theoretical findings.
infographic.watch_item: Projection-free updates allow unit-length deviations, and the limiting energy inequality requires additional assumptions on the energy functional.
infographic.paper_title: A decoupled BDF2-type integrator for the spin-diffusion Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert system in ferromagnetic multilayers

title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning
authors: Antonio Varagnolo, Miaomiao Dai, Bolei Deng, Raphaël Pestourie
abstract: Designing mechanical metamaterials for nonlinear behavior such as energy absorption is limited by high-dimensional parametrizations and by expensive simulations. Here we show that design knowledge from a cheap linear property can be transferred to nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable, targets through a learned, reusable search space. TRAMA (TRAnsferable representation learning for Metamaterial Architectures) reparametrizes architected materials using a variational autoencoder with a pre-trained vision transformer and physics-informed augmentations. For energy-absorption efficiency, TRAMA reaches every efficiency level with 95 to 98% reduction in the evaluations needed by state-of-the-art gradient-free optimization and 3 to 5 fewer than gradient-based optimization. Its best design is comparable to the best found by any baseline with at least 67% fewer evaluations, which translate into approximately 100 hours saved per campaign with finite-element simulations. Fabricated designs match simulated stress-strain curves within 5.3%. A post hoc analysis shows where the representation transfers to new properties and where it does not.

infographic.key_insight: TRAMA transfers knowledge from a cheap linear property into a reusable learned design space for optimizing nonlinear mechanical metamaterial behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces costly simulation-driven searches for energy-absorbing architectures, saving approximately 100 hours per finite-element optimization campaign.
method: Learn an architectural representation using a variational autoencoder with a pre-trained vision transformer.
Use physics-informed augmentations to support representation learning.
Transfer the learned search space to nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable design objectives.
infographic.evidence_signal: For energy-absorption efficiency, TRAMA required 95–98% fewer evaluations than state-of-the-art gradient-free optimization, while fabricated designs matched simulated stress–strain curves within 5.3%.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability is property-dependent; the learned representation may not benefit every new objective.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning
